blocks.x: Ed Garland April 16th 1957 real one
interview with Ed Garland in Hollywood and we're just talking you're telling me why they called

you want to do well there was a fellow used to come in the club called by the name of Monti he used to give us lots of tips and the boys used to laugh at him because he was very comical old fella and we begin to call each other Monti well nobody would laugh it off when it come down to me call me Monti I got hot about it I didn't like it so from there on they begin to call me Monti and I always want to jump on the whole bed the guitar player what that was this kid ory in New York you say who was on there yeah it was in New York did you play with or in New York yeah we went to New York to play when was that well that was about uh if I can recall it 19
How did you happen to leave New Orleans? What happened? Well, Freddie Keppert was playing for a girl by the name they called Mabel Elaine.
In New Orleans?

No. Mabel Elaine and her jazz band. She's a white girl. She used to clunk band. You know how Boa Jingles used to dance with wooden shoes on. She had the same thing. She used to be in a bale of cotton. She was blackface. When you get on the stage, that bale of cotton was out there. They couldn't go out. We'd be all lying around in this cotton, see, with a couple of holes on, satin cover holes, different colors, and bandana, hangers, and hats. So I had, when we started playing, this fave of cotton opened up. And she'd come out there. It was a pretty good show. Was this on the stage? On the stage. We were on off in time. Yeah. Mabel Elaine and her jazz band. And this big boat was the Robert E. Lee. This was in Chicago? That's why I thought it was Mabel Elaine. No. Well, that's how I come to go to Chicago. Freddie's telling you, Freddie Keppert was playing for him. Freddie and them got to New York. He got a job in New York or something, and he quit. And this man sent for another band. Then Manuel Perez come out with a bunch. But then they said, I come right behind Manuel Perez and them, and went with this girl, Mabel Elaine. And then they said, I'm a little bit. I brought Sugar Johnny, trumpet, Louis Keppert on guitar, Roy Palmer on trombone, Herbert Lindsay on violin, and a boy named Lawrence Duell on clarinet, myself on bass. And I had Happy to play drum, and just as we were fixed, Happy was fixed to get on the train, here comes the telegram. And the agent down there, you know, the man who was looking out for us, setting us off, he said, Stop Happy called me, he came in and told him, I said, Don't bring the drummer. Poor little Happy like to die. Just fixed to get up on the train with his drums, you know, at the Union Station in New Orleans. I would have New Orleans.
This is in 1912?
Yeah, he fixed to get on this thing.
Was it your band where you lead drove the band?
Me, I was the head of the band. So we went on, and we left Mabel Elaine, out there. The show closed, that's what it was. Now they go on their vacation.
Well, did you go on the train to Chicago?
Yeah, yeah.
Straight to Chicago?
Right to Chicago, on the other one, to Illinois. Illinois, I said.
Uh-huh. And when you got there, where did you start to play in Chicago?

I went to Mabel Elaine, the show. Then we come back to Chicago, later on Chicago there, for a while, you understand. We got to go around different nightclubs, so they heard about the band. I went to work. Oh, you know, they got over there what they call Blue Mondays, Blue Wednesdays. Every nightclub has got a day. What is that? Yeah, the day, like, like they got just now, they call it a jam session. Well, all right, Blue Monday, all right, your place is closed. All your entertainers would go to the next club that day and do numbers, you know, sing or something, you know. You come in, anybody, you know, bands. All right, we went over to Deluxe, and everybody was crazy about me slapping their bass, you know. All right. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Oh, yeah? In San Francisco? Yeah. It was upstairs street. But Dreamland was the one, and it was a pretty nice place. Across the street from there.
What part of Chicago was the Deluxe?

35th and State. It was upstairs over to old Panama. The Panama used to be right on the corner of 35th and State. A couple of doors over this way was the pool hall upstairs. Then next to it upstairs was the Deluxe.
Did they have stage shows too there? Flo shows or anything like that? Yeah. At the Deluxe?
There's not no floor shows. No, just floor girls sing on the floor because there wasn't nothing there for them to do. They danced right out there on the floor, you see?
There were big girls there?

No, no, no, no, no. There wasn't no big girls there, no. Dancing? Dancing and entertaining. Billy Bottoms had the same thing across the way. Then Billy Bottoms, they all got crazy about the jazz band. I could get a job all around. The first time I went to the union, all right, here come the walking delegate now. The walking delegate come up, talking about, I have to join the union. I said, you crazy. I ain't stood about no union. You ain't going to mess me up. You all need to join the union so you can take me off this job or take me out of. Have your favorites and I'll be around you and won't have no job. You got to join the job everybody, you know. All them waiters is union, you see? I'll argue with them. I said, come back again. I said, well, all right. We'll give you another week. This week you're going to join the union or you can come out of here. They told Shaw that he was going to pull all the waiters out. I said, Mr. Shaw, I said, golly, come here tomorrow and I ain't going to meet you. I don't know what he's going to want me for. I goes over there and he gives me a check. He's going out of the union. I said, for what? He said, he got to join the union. I said, all right, take this check. Go down up here for the boys. I went down and I won't show you. I can show you right now. I think I got the proof right here. I got out of the union. We joined the union. Everything was all right. So, I've been in the union ever since. What is it? Now, this is something there I should have this. That's what you call a traveling transfer. A transfer. When I went to Frisco with King Oliver, who went to number six, was playing 피cola. That was in 1920. That's your transfer. Now that'll tell you when I read it out. You and you did.
Yes. I'm trying to. Pull that loose. I'm not tearing it. You see, Copeland was second time.
It says July 1st, 1921. Well, that's when I got that transfer. Oh.
This is later. Oh, well, it was just I've been in the years. July 1st, 1921.
Well, you've been on the West Coast. I didn't want to know.
This is much later.

That's when, that's one, that's a transfer when I left, you see. We left in 20. Uh-huh. And come to Frisco, that's when I want. Now you look, you see number six. You can see the local number six, that's in Frisco. Yes. Well, how long did you stay in Chicago?
What happened after the Deluxe?

Oh, I stayed, I stayed, I stayed in the Deluxe three, four years or more. Then, two years and something. Because Billy Bottoms got me to come over to Dreamland, see. Just before I went to the Dreamland, uh, Basie come to Chicago with, uh, P.R. this woman who called, oh, it was already a TV time, uh, show, what's that called? Come there with a show and a heart, and I went and got Basie. I stole Basie and bought Basie up to the Deluxe side to do it.
Is that so? Yeah.
Then the next time.
What did they call that band? The band at Deluxe. What, what, what was the name of the band at the Deluxe?
Oh, Garland's New Orleans Jazz Band.
Oh yeah? Garland's New Orleans Jazz Band. Uh-huh. Jazz band, yeah.

Then, uh, Johnny Dodds come in town. We got a hold of Johnny Dodds. Nora Dutre was in the neighborhood. He used to come into Chicago and he'd come sit in with us. So, uh, Boyd H. Williams opened up the, uh, the, opened up this club on 34th Street, uh, Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland And Joe comes in, all right? Joe gets Bill Johnson to play bass with him. He got a woman named Lottie, she was playing violin, and some other woman was playing piano. Bursar? No, no. We didn't get a whole bunch until we come out here. Oh, I did. First of all. Then we began to get in our band together. See, we got our heads together that we're going to get our aunt group. We finally got Noah Dutrae and Johnny, you see, myself. Ram come in town, I had Baby Hall play with me, his brother. Ram come in, he was running on the railroad. You mean Tubby Hall? Tubby was playing with me, but Ram was running on the SP, the dishwasher there. Oh, yeah? Yeah. He was cooking dishwash in the house. Uh-huh. Then, after we got the bunch together, after he went to war, to the army, he come back. I takes Ram. Then finally Joe goes away. He gets all together, organized our regular group. We had Noah Dutrae, we had Jimmy Pilar, Johnny Dodge, Lil, I got Lil to play with me, Lil Hardin, her name. Lil Armstrong, she's waking for Mrs. Jones. She's music, you know, demonstrating. Yes. I had a job on the west side in Chicago, and I asked her, could I use her for that night? I said, oh no, you want to steal my girl? I said, oh, this one for the night, they don't want no guitar. Lil kept playing guitar, you see. The man said, you better get your piano to play if you want to stay around here and wait. You can be playing away because you'll get your piano to play. I kept on listening to Lil Hardin.
Was it hard to find a piano player at the time?

No, I got a hold of Lil. It wasn't hard. So Lil said, yeah, I'll go play with you. We went to play for a Chinese restaurant, along the west side. So the man gave me the job he liked bad. He said, I could have this job. So I said, Silvio, you want to work with it? Sure. I said, what do you want to tell Mrs. Jones? I ain't stood by Mrs. Jones.
Oh, yeah. I said, well, what do you want to tell your mother? Well, I'll tell her I'm playing someone for a church affair.

That's honest before God, she's telling her much she's playing for a church affair. The whole time she prayed there. You know, the church affair last all this time. I went on to her, Mrs. Jones. I said, Mrs. Jones wants to play with me. I told you she was going to steal my guts. I didn't steal her.

She said she wanted to play with the jazz band. She said, it's all right, Eddie. I'm glad she's gone. Glad for you to have her. Was pay better in Chicago than in New Orleans? Oh, sure. Was much? Oh, sure. Was there a big difference in what you could earn?
No, a big difference in day and night.
Well, how so?
Look, you play down the district. Now, all right. Go down there, you play from 9 o'clock, 4 o'clock in the month, of course, you make tips. You got only a dollar and a half of that.
For when that's what?

The next work, down the course, but you can do so much with that dollar and a half, though. You understand, Nick? Sure. Well, you got up to Chicago, you see. You got more money than Chicago. And this is thick now in Chicago. Next time, when the rule is getting, they get 18, 18, 17, 1850 and 25 hours a week. Uh-huh. In Chicago, you see.
That's much different, sir.
It's much different. In New Orleans, you only pay two dollars a week for a room in New Orleans. Couldn't pay no two dollars a week for no room out this way. Yeah.
Is that one of the reasons why I went to Chicago? Because pay was higher? Pay was higher.

And in the beginning, they're getting that after we got on there, Freddie Kemper and myself, and, and, uh, Marion Perrin's, we got on in, up there. And that's where the jazz, the Dixie, the jazz band. In other words, uh, they call it, uh, the jazz band.
Original, original Creole band.
The Creole band went over big, and the people was falling for that, you know, but the kids were coming out. I, I, I...

Was that the first band that went out of New Orleans? Freddie Kemper. Freddie Kemper's Creole band. Yeah. What they call the original Creole band. The original Creole band. And was the first one that left... That's the band. Freddie Kemper. The first one that went to Chicago, huh? Did they go to Chicago or New York?
They, they come right to Chicago first. Yeah. No, Chicago. No, they come to Chicago. You see?
That was about 1912 or 1911 or something like that? Let me see what that was.

That must have been around the first part. Around in, around in that time. Yeah, it was. Because, uh, Freddie and them left. Because when they left, they had Cantrell, not Cantrell, they had, uh, Freddie Kemper, and they had, uh, Eddie Vincent on trombone. And they had, uh...
And wasn't Dink Johnson in that band?

No. No. No. No. Dink Johnson brought to the band out after they was out there, you know, where they used to bass. Dink Johnson's brother, their brother played guitar by ours one played guitar. Uh-huh. They had him.
See? That's where that happened.

Then the next band went, Big Eye Lewy. He come along. Big Eye Lewy was with Freddie and, uh, and-and-and-and George Backe was with, uh, And, uh, George Fields was with Manuel. Then when I was at the Dreamland, I went to Wake Down and Peekin for Dan Jackson, and I used to have Manuel, Teo, Frankie Enya, see, and, uh, Eddie Atkins on some bones.
You mean Lorenzo Teo?

Lorenzo Teo, you see. Was playing clarinet. I played bass. Then the Dixon Land, the original Dixon Land, uh, jazz band from New Orleans, white boys, Dixon Land 5, we played on Madison and Paulina on the west side, the Osonia. They in one corner was another corner.
Oh, yeah? You mean the same place? In the same place.
One band? One band? I was down amongst them gangsters. It was awful around there. What was the name of that club?
Yussonia.
Yussonia. Yeah. Madison and Palermo. Madison and Palermo?
Palermo, Palermo. Madison and Palermo.
Uh-huh. That's one of them rough ones, you see.
Was it a big club? Yeah. What was that, about 1915 or something?
That was around in that time, yeah. Or whatever they were.
And on one side there was this band that you described? Two bands, two bands played in the air. You mean not from the same bandstand?
No, no.
Across from each other. Yeah, we had our own stand. You had your bandstand. Yeah, they had their own stand, yeah. They had their own stand, and they would dance floor in the middle?
You see, Monkey was playing drums with them, that's what they called him, Monkey, and he blowed in the kazoo. Kazoo. They didn't have no, uh, they didn't have no, uh, trumpet.
They had no trumpets? No, the Dixielands, they didn't have the old raguums.
No, they didn't have no trumpet. They drum is a prayer like kazoo.
What, what were the five pieces in the Dixielands that had there?
Uh, they had a clarinet, they had trombone, piano. Drums? Drums. And they had another piece. I said, I wish for a high. They didn't have no trumpet. Perfect. This God was his good prayer, though.
Was it a good band?
Yeah, they were in the Dixielands. Were they swinging?
Sure, they always from the islands.
Sure they could swing.
That was a tough place. Huh? That was a tough place. That was a tough place. Yeah, it was a tough place, alright, and didn't worry us. But I mean, they're down there amongst them gangsters, you know.
Did they have a lot of fights down there? Oh, yeah, they get to fighting down there. Yeah. Were they hustlers and so on? Yeah. Hustlers? Oh, everything down there.
Everything was down there. Oh, boy.
Well, they made a lot of money down there, though. Was that place run by a bunch of gangsters? I don't know. This is Ed Garland.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you. Everything was down there.
Oh, boy. Well, it was a lot of money down there, though. Was that place run by a bunch of gangsters? I don't know. This is Ed Garland.
I want to.
Thank you. Thank you.
Thank you.
The original bass player, the first man to pluck a bass. You know, they were all bowing the bass. Yeah. First man to start it. Really? First man in history to start that.
Still around.
He was playing in 1905. Famous New Orleans musician. The greatest of all time. He's my old buddy. He's telling us a wonderful, you know. You're rolling. Yeah, I know. That's all right.
It's very interesting. Oh, yeah.

In places like the Deluxe and the Royal Garden in Chicago, you know. Yeah. Did you, were, were the audience, white or Negro? Both. Both. They mixed. They mixed. Yeah. Yeah. But was it more one than the other?
Well, in fact, it was more Negroes, you know.
But down to the Deluxe, they always had a pretty fair group of whites. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Were there, were there any musicians from Chicago who came to listen to you?

Oh, my goodness. Oh, my goodness. Yeah, a gang of them. Show all of them, all them boys out to theaters. Yeah. That time, you used to have them. But he's talking, too, so just leave. At that time, you used to have them in the band. Huh? At that time in the theaters, you know, they was playing in the pitch, you know, they were playing in the pitch, you know. Yeah. And all the boys used to come down, they'd only hear that jazz music, you know. They didn't play no jazz music. See? They came to get some ideas for you. Sure, that's right.
Same way in Frisco, when we come to Frisco.
And when did you first come out the West Coast? Well, it's like I told you, the first time I come to the West Coast, when I was in Tennessee 10 in 17. 1917.
Then I come back again to the West Coast in 20, 21, no, 20, out to Frisco, to the Deluxe.

What band were you with then? King Oliver. King Oliver. King Oliver. King Oliver. King Oliver. King Oliver's Nine Kings. There were nine pieces? Nine. It's a pretty big band, huh? Well, we had Jimmy Ballard played violin and tempo for Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to What band were you with then? King Oliver. We went there with King Oliver's Nine Kings. There were nine pieces?
There were nine. It's a pretty big band, huh?
Well, we had Jimmy Pallar played violin and tenor saxophone, and we had Jones playing mellophone and alto.
David Jones?

David Jones playing alto, mellophone and sax. We had Johnny Dots playing clarinet. We had Lilian Armstrong on piano. We had Minor Hall on drums, and we had Notre Dutre on trombone, and myself on bass, and King Oliver was playing. That's the way the band was picked up when we went to Frisco, playing at the Procola dance hall.
And when you came west, did you plan to stay here, or did you just come for a short trip? Well, we come to play that engagement, that's all.

No, we come to play that engagement, and when the Procola fooled up, we went over to Oakland, and I got a job over there from Lucious for the band. Joe told me to go ahead, I did the band. I don't know, something was wrong. Joe had gotten in a little trouble with the union, so I taken a job over at the, uh, at the, uh,
Creole Cafe. When you came to the west coast, did they know about jazz here, did they? No.
Were you one of the first bands? Yeah, I didn't know about no jazz.
Were there any other people who were playing that kind of music?
No. Still, the Prod and them had the best band around there at the right time. That was at, uh, Leicester Mapp's place.
Was that in the city of San Francisco?
Yeah, over there, in Jackson. Yeah. Coiny?
On the barbaco's. Yeah. I was. You remember a fellow named, uh, did you know a fellow named Beansy? Foray? Beansy? Uh, Gammler? Yeah.
Sure, I know Beansy well. I know his wife, Nancy. She's running around with Nancy.
We saw him over down there.
Beansy used to be a big shot in the all, and they had a gambling place. Now, he's down there now.
Yeah?
We saw him.

Yeah? Yes. I was asking him about, uh, Um, were you ever, were you ever in Lula White's show? I've been trying to figure out how the girls used to dress, you know, when they came down to the parlor and were sitting around. All right. They came down to the parlor, they had, um, those beautiful little dresses on.

Looked like a little baby, you know? You ever see a little baby when they put some clothes on a baby? Kidding how they kind of stuck up? Oh, like that, you know. All silk, you know. And these stockings, like I'm telling you. That time used to have what they called lace stockings. You know, open-led stockings. And these big bows on them, you know. And their hair all fixed up. They could see everything all just low, you know.
It was kind of a cut low.
Yeah, they could see everything. And some of them used to have a big bull ribbon on the back of the head, you know.
Were these special dresses that they had made for themselves? Oh, sure. They weren't ordinary store dresses.

Oh, no, no. Some of those, the same as a bottle of dress for a little 10-year-old, 11-year-old kid. Not maybe smaller than that. The thing was way over the need. They just was part of the monkey, that's all.
That's all. You understand?

That's all. Then you go down there, and you sit and follow your professor. He's playing over there. Lula's house has mirrors all around. See? Mirrors? Mirrors, yeah. And all different little freak lights. All colors. See?
You mean there are mirrors all over the world?

All over. All around. Yeah. And piano, he's sitting over there playing. Professor, they say, the professor. All right, they have blue ribbon beer. Bottle beer. You got a mayday. She don't do nothing but handle that beer. Lula didn't have to contact her. So many cases of beer. She goes by the bottles. All right, that may when you want something to drink. If you'd order up maybe five bottles of beer. That was five dollars. Five bottles of beer, that's five dollars. The beer one cost you a quarter. Big one.
Uh-huh. What was that for a quart?
Blue ribbon, yeah.
Big, big bottle? Yeah. One dollar. What kind of freak lighting did they have in there?

Well, there's different colored lights, you understand? It's like on the theater, you can shade your lights, you understand? Did they change all blue? You can dim them. You can dim them. You can turn on all blue, blue and red, white, you know, like that, you know?
Were they changing all the time, or did they just?
No, this was one color there. Just those lights and the mirrors, you know? Seemed flicking like, you know?
Did you ever work there?

Huh? Did you work there? No, nothing but piano. Yeah, I already telling people about he was there. He know much about Lula White as you do. I'm not telling you no story. He was out there in the country, pig and peas. I heard that woman come talking about, Ed used to go with her. I said, go with who? I said, Ed don't know Lula White if he's here. He used to go with her. George Lambert was old man, a big gambler. I had the gambling house on Cronlet, on St. Charles, between Petita and the foot of Petita, between Petita and Padres, upstairs. Big gambling house. I used to carry clothes there.
Who was the piano player at the Lula White? Who played there? Well, there were several different fellas.
That one time, Jelly Rolls played there, and then Albert Cal played there.
Did you ever hear of a guy whose name is Manuel Mineta? Manuel Mineta, sure. Do you know him?

Oh, yeah. Manuel Mineta played violin and piano. Played trumpet. He's teaching now. We saw him. We spent a lot of time with him. He's teaching music now. He's a little over in Algiers. That's right. I don't know Manuel. Call him horse.
A lot of people still call him horse.
Yeah. Did he play at Lulu's? He played down the district, yeah. He used to play, I think he played for Mimicristine down there on the basement between Conard and Bianbo.
I still don't quite understand. These were like little girl, little kids' dresses. Starched. Do you mean they stuck out?
Oh, and I'll tell you. You ever see a ballet dancer?
Yeah.
Oh, you see them little dresses they have on?
Yeah.
Well, they'll know what they're at.
I see. I see. Because people say that they were real stylish, you know?
No, not those people. I wasn't no real stylish. Because when they come in there, they come in there with that little short dress, you understand? Yeah.
Those long stockers?

Yeah. And those stockers on in a great big bowl. See, they had them garters, you know. They put on in a big bowl on each side. See? How was the top of them cut? Were they just— Oh, that's kind of open. Right. You know, you see a person wearing a waist, a woman wearing these waist, a woman wearing a little lower all down in here, you know. You could see pretty much everything. Yeah, sure. They wasn't nude all around. They just could see all the things.
They wear anything under those dresses or just the dresses? Oh, yeah.
They wore things under those panties on them. Them big, big red drawers, you know, with lace all on them.
Yeah. So, could lace all on them, you understand? So, were they mostly light-skinned girls? Uh, Lula. Lula had all kinds, hock-to-roons, uh, white.
You understand?
Were they white girls working there, too? Yeah, white girls, yeah. I assumed they didn't wear brassieres, did they?
Uh, I don't know. I don't remember. No, I don't think they did.
I wouldn't think so.

No, because this was open. You could see down there. Now, they had any type of woman you want. But the ugliest woman they had in there was the prettiest. What do you mean by that? Well, I mean by that there wasn't nothing ugly in there.
Oh, I see.
No, no. Nothing ugly in there.
Everything old man was pretty. Then they asked the evil thing. Was it expensive to make it with those girls? Oh, yeah.

You know, no, no, man. You tried? No. Oh, try what? I'd better not try to go in there. It looked like I want to go there for anything. No? I started bringing a message. Then they come talking about the oil. They said, go with her. Shit. I used to bring George Lambert. I used to bring the clothes there for George Lambert. This man from a big gambling house. Used to bring what? Clothes. The wife from nice. Now tell me something.

Were all the customers, you know, the people used to go, the sports who went there to, you know, to spend some time with the girls. Were they all white people who went to the boys? Yes, right. All white people.
No sound boy had no chains going there.
No, huh? No.
When he'd go there for less, he was a poor to go in there to haul some bottles away from there or something.
That's the only time he was there. Well, where would they go? Oh, they had plenty of places. Oh, they had plenty of places.
For that, all up and down Corn Eye Street. All up and down Corn Eye Street. All up. All up and down Corn Eye Street. All up and down Corn Eye Street.
The End The End
Ed Garland, April 16, 1957, reel 3.
That broke him off for a while, though. That boy hit him inside the nose. Did you slow him down a little bit?
Did it?

He hit him, too. I don't blame him. He's a pretty old girl. I wasn't that bad. I got into Humberg and Rick Charles. Two cousins was fighting. I called myself trying to separate them and they thought I was interfering, gonna get in and help them and they hauled off and they beat me half to death, both of them. I also I said, man, what are you doing? I said, I'm trying to separate you boys. I don't care who it is. I don't want to see you boys fighting.
I don't want to see you boys fighting.
I said, I want to kill you. I said, I want to kill you.
I said, I want to do it out there.

Everybody on the best and I'm out there and I want to try to stop them boys from fighting. They black by. Me and Johnny Dodd took a fight every night. Really? Every night. We'd get the kid and get the best of them first thing in the fight. Right after the affair was over, we'd all go down there. Down probably we'd go down to the Pacawas or go somewhere to the Eagle Saloon drink and give us some oil saloon. Then we forgot all about the fight. Throw nobody in the fear though.
Fight every night.

You and Johnny? Mm-hmm. What'd you fight about? You and Johnny say, start the kid and get the best of one another. They call me that Montutti, you know, and I didn't want them to call me that. I was playing in the Al Jays, a funeral for the odd fellas. There was twelve of us. And I'm back there, playing the bass drum. Come on, Montutti, what's the matter? I said, who you talking to? Come on, hit that drum, man. You're going to be tired. I'll be arguing over there, that guy.
